  4. Stadium Sukuk (Proposal)

Proposal

In this proposal, a stadium is financed through Sukuk while the landowner keeps the land.

HAYKALAH proposed this framework in 2026. It is a proposal with no mandate, and its figures are withheld until the source documents are reconciled.

A stadium needs capital long before it earns. In 2026 HAYKALAH proposed a Sukuk framework for stadium precincts that combines three Shariah contracts: Musataha rights over the land, Istisna’a during construction, then Ijara or Wakala-Ijara once the stadium is complete. There is one issuer per stadium, across seven precincts for 2034. This explainer steps through the framework as proposed. It is a proposal, not a mandate.

Step by step

Step 1 of 6

Proposal

The issuer takes Musataha rights over the land.

The landowner grants the issuer the right to build on and use the land for an agreed term, and keeps title throughout. The framework proposes one issuer for each stadium.

  • Landowner to Issuer, one per stadium Musataha: right to build on and use the land for an agreed term

All steps

  1. 01The issuer takes Musataha rights over the land.

    The landowner grants the issuer the right to build on and use the land for an agreed term, and keeps title throughout. The framework proposes one issuer for each stadium.

    • Landowner to Issuer, one per stadium Musataha: right to build on and use the land for an agreed term

  2. 02A Shariah board approves the structure.

    Before any Sukuk are issued, a Shariah board reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents. HAYKALAH does not maintain its own Shariah board; where the issuer has none, HAYKALAH can arrange an independent one.

    • Shariah board to Issuer, one per stadium Review and approval of the contracts, the asset and the documents

  3. 03Sukuk holders provide the capital.

    The Sukuk are offered to investors through an appropriately licensed institution, because offering Sukuk is a regulated activity. HAYKALAH does not issue, offer or deal in securities.

    • Licensed institution to Sukuk holders Offers the Sukuk (regulated activity)
    • Sukuk holders to Issuer, one per stadium Sukuk proceeds

  4. 04Istisna’a funds the construction.

    The issuer orders the stadium to an agreed specification under an Istisna’a, and the price can be paid in stages while it is built. The contractor who builds it can work under a separate, parallel Istisna’a.

    • Issuer, one per stadium to Contractor Price paid in stages during construction
    • Contractor to Issuer, one per stadium Stadium built to the agreed specification

  5. 05The completed stadium is leased.

    Once the stadium is complete, it moves to an Ijara, or to a Wakala-Ijara in which an agent procures the asset that is then leased. The lessee pays rent for the use of the stadium, and the issuer, as lessor, keeps the responsibilities of ownership that the contract and the applicable Shariah standards assign to it.

    • Issuer, one per stadium to Lessee Ijara or Wakala-Ijara: use of the stadium for an agreed term
    • Lessee to Issuer, one per stadium Rent

  6. 06The rent pays the Sukuk holders.

    The rent funds periodic distributions to the Sukuk holders. The landowner keeps title to the land throughout, and the Musataha contract sets what happens to the buildings when its term ends.

    • Lessee to Issuer, one per stadium Rent
    • Issuer, one per stadium to Sukuk holders Periodic distributions from the rent

The parties

Landowner
Grants the Musataha rights and keeps title to the land
Issuer, one per stadium
A special purpose vehicle that holds the rights and the stadium for the Sukuk holders
Shariah board
Reviews and approves the contracts, the asset and the documents
Licensed institution
Offers the Sukuk to investors, a regulated activity
Sukuk holders
Provide the capital and receive distributions from the rent
Contractor
Builds the stadium to the agreed specification
Lessee
Leases and uses the completed stadium

Who it suits

  • Public owners of land that want venues built and financed without selling the land.

  • Programs with several venues, where one issuer per stadium keeps each stadium’s rights, contracts and income in its own vehicle.

  • Banks and financial institutions that review Sukuk frameworks for public assets with their own Shariah board.

Risks and conditions

  • It is a proposal. There is no mandate, and no figures are shown until the source documents are reconciled.

  • Approvals come first. No structure is final until a Shariah board approves it, and offering the Sukuk needs a licensed institution and the regulatory approvals that apply.

  • Construction comes before income. The stadium earns nothing until it is built, so the specification, the price and the delivery date in the Istisna’a matter.

  • The distributions depend on the rent. Sukuk holders are paid from the rent, so they depend on the lessee paying it under the lease.

  • The rights have an end date. The Musataha runs for an agreed term, and its contract sets what happens to the buildings when the term ends.

  • No guarantee of approvals, financing or returns.
